extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, math educators, researchers in philosophy/psychology of mathematics, and anyone who evaluates mathematical proofs (e.g., Math Stack Exchange users)
extracted.subtask_description: A rubric/instrument for appraising mathematical proofs across empirically derived, statistically separable dimensions (aesthetics, intricacy, utility, precision). Useful for scoring or discussing proof quality without conflating distinct qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: The aesthetic dimension (beauty, elegance, profundity) captured by adjectives such as 'beautiful, elegant, profound, inspired, charming, ingenious, sublime, deep.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures perceived beauty/elegance of a proof. Inglis & Aberdein found this is a distinct factor from simplicity and often correlates mildly with intricacy; do not assume brevity or minimal hypotheses are required for a proof to be rated high on aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intricacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The intricacy/complexity dimension captured by adjectives such as 'complicated, intricate, elaborate, dense, sophisticated' (with 'deep' loading weakly here).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures complexity, elaboration, and density of a proof. Note that many proofs judged beautiful are also judged intricate; intricacy is empirically separable from precision/rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The utility/usefulness dimension captured by adjectives such as 'useful, applicable, fertile, fruitful, informative, generative.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures how useful or applicable a proof is (e.g., yields corollaries, methods, or further work). Utility is largely independent from aesthetics — a proof can be useful without being judged beautiful, and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision
rubrics_metrics.description: The precision/rigor dimension captured by adjectives such as 'careful, meticulous, rigorous, exact, detailed, formal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures technical correctness, rigor, and formal exactness. Distinguish this from mere detail or elaboration: detail can load on intricacy rather than precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inglis–Aberdein 16-adjective scale (practical instrument)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 16-item Likert instrument composed of 4 adjectives for each of the four dimensions: Aesthetics (beautiful, elegant, profound, inspired), Intricacy (intricate, complicated, elaborate, sophisticated), Utility (useful, applicable, fruitful, informative), Precision (precise, meticulous, rigorous, careful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the four adjectives per dimension as items on a Likert scale and aggregate (e.g., average) to obtain scores for each axis. The instrument is designed for empirical appraisal and comparative studies of proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score each axis independently
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the four axes (Aesthetics, Intricacy, Utility, Precision) as orthogonal/separable dimensions when evaluating proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a proof, provide separate ratings for each axis rather than a single global 'good/bad' label. The factors capture different qualities and should not be conflated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty is not simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not equate beauty with simplicity; Inglis & Aberdein's headline finding is that 'Aesthetics and simplicity are largely uncorrelated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming that a shorter or more minimal-hypotheses proof is necessarily more beautiful. Empirically, beauty correlates mildly positively with intricacy for many mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate detail with rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Detail/elaboration is not the same as precision/rigor — detail tends to load on the intricacy factor, not precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A verbose or elaborate proof may feel intricate without being more rigorous; likewise a concise proof may be precise. Evaluate 'precision' items (rigorous, exact, meticulous) separately from 'intricacy' items (elaborate, dense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility and beauty are independent
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful and beautiful are separable qualities; a proof can be useful without being judged beautiful, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing for or assessing a proof, state both its utility (applications, generative power) and its aesthetic qualities independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and account for disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic appraisals of proofs show substantial individual variation; between-rater correlations for beauty are modest (~0.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat single raters' aesthetic judgments as informative but not definitive. Recognize social influences on judgments and that lack of consensus is normal; use aggregated scores or report variation when possible.
